lead: A protocol is the rulebook for messages; a standard is an agreed written version of that rulebook. IoT devices from different vendors need both. Without shared rules they cannot exchange even a temperature reading. Standards appear in homes, factories, smart cities and farms.
prereq: You need: Unit 1, logical design and communication models.

blocks.text: A protocol is a set of rules for messages: which side sends, in what order, what fields appear, and what a reply means. A standard is a written agreement that many vendors follow. They are not the same: a standard can leave many features optional, and a de facto protocol can dominate the market with no formal standard. IoT needs standards because a sensor, a phone and a cloud service often come from different vendors. Interoperability means they exchange a reading without a custom adapter for every pair. Metcalfe's law says the value of a network grows with the square of its users, so each compatible device helps every existing user.

De jure standards come from a recognized body. De facto standards come from market use first, with formal text later or never. A buyer should ask which is which, because a de facto protocol may have no conformance test. A profile is a smaller list of mandatory options chosen from a broad standard. Profiles matter in IoT because a full standard may not fit a small device.

A common IoT stack has five layers, described here from the top down. The application layer holds MQTT and CoAP; these are message styles, not radios. The transport layer uses TCP or UDP. The network layer uses IPv6, often compressed by 6LoWPAN. The MAC layer uses IEEE 802.15.4 or Bluetooth Low Energy. The PHY layer is the radio itself. When a message is sent, each layer adds its own header to the payload. The receiver removes the headers in reverse order. This is encapsulation. Links to the detailed standards are in IEEE 802.15.4, 6LoWPAN and Bluetooth Low Energy.

Layering lets one layer change without rewriting the others. A new radio can carry the same MQTT message. A gateway can translate between two stacks: it terminates one stack and opens another. The cost is header bytes. Constrained devices have small frames, so every byte matters. The frame formats are in later chapters.

blocks.where: S is the final packet size in bytes; P is the application payload in bytes; hᵢ is the header added by layer i in bytes; the sum runs over all layers that add a header.

sections.h3: Standardization in practice, and its pain points

blocks.text: Standardization has practical problems. Too many options: a standard may define ten ways to do one job, and two compliant devices may still not talk. Profiles fix this by making one choice mandatory. IPR is another problem: a standard may include patented technology, and a small vendor must know the licensing terms before shipping. Security is often optional in older IoT standards, so a product can be compliant and still unprotected. Constrained devices cannot carry full web stacks, so compression and small buffers are needed. Gateways translate between incompatible stacks, but they add cost and a single point of failure. Some syllabi call this protocol standardization for IoT.

items: M2M protocols are examples of device-to-server messaging.
WSN protocols are examples of sensor-network routing.
SCADA protocols are examples of industrial supervision; see industrial protocols.
RFID protocols are examples of tag reading; see Unit 2.

blocks.text: A common exam question asks why standards do not remove gateways. Installed devices follow different generations and profiles; a gateway is cheaper than replacing them.

examples.question: A 4-layer IoT protocol stack adds 2 bytes at layer 1, 4 bytes at layer 2, 8 bytes at layer 3 and 20 bytes at layer 4. The application payload is 100 bytes. What is the total header overhead in bytes and as a percentage of the final packet?
examples.answer: The total header overhead is 34 bytes; the final packet is 134 bytes; overhead is 25.4% of the final packet.
examples.check:
h = 2 + 4 + 8 + 20
packet = 100 + h
pct = round(100 * h / packet, 1)
print(h)
print(packet)
print(pct)

traps: A protocol is not automatically a standard. A de facto protocol can have no formal standard, and a standard can contain many optional features.
Do not call a market leader a de jure standard. De jure means a recognized standards body produced the text.
More layers add header bytes. A 100-byte payload does not stay 100 bytes on the wire.
Overhead percentage uses the final packet as the denominator, not the application payload.
A compliant device is not always a secure device. Older IoT standards often make security optional.

quiz.q: Define protocol and standard. Give one difference between them.
quiz.a: A protocol is a set of message rules: order, fields and meaning. A standard is an agreed written version of rules. A standard can leave features optional, while a protocol may be de facto with no formal standard.

quiz.q: Name four standards bodies and one IoT protocol or family for each.
quiz.a: IETF, CoAP; IEEE, 802.15.4; LoRa Alliance, LoRaWAN; Connectivity Standards Alliance, Matter.

quiz.q: Why does a profile exist in IoT standardization?
quiz.a: A broad standard has many optional features, so two compliant devices may not interoperate. A profile selects a mandatory subset. This reduces choices and fits small devices.

quiz.q: What does a gateway do when two IoT stacks differ?
quiz.a: It terminates one stack, translates the message and opens the other stack. It hides differences but adds cost, latency and a possible single point of failure.

quiz.q: A 3-layer stack adds 3 bytes at layer 1, 5 bytes at layer 2 and 10 bytes at layer 3. The payload is 80 bytes. Find the header overhead in bytes and as a percentage of the final packet.
quiz.a: Overhead = 3 + 5 + 10 = 18 bytes. Final packet = 80 + 18 = 98 bytes. Percentage = (18 / 98) × 100 = 18.37%, rounded to 18.4%.

quiz.q: A vendor says its device is standard-compliant but not secure. How is this possible, and what should a buyer ask?
quiz.a: The standard may make security optional or may define profiles without security. The buyer should ask which profile is implemented, whether security is mandatory, what certification exists and what IPR terms apply.

quiz.q: Why can too many standards slow IoT adoption? Use de jure and de facto standards and profiles in your answer.
quiz.a: Many de jure standards and de facto products create fragmentation. Buyers wait for a winner, and vendors build gateways. Profiles help only when the market adopts them. Too many profiles recreate the same problem.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, Matter and Thread push IP into home devices, while oneM2M appears in large M2M deployments. Researchers work on semantic interoperability and on profiles for constrained devices. Search for Matter specification, oneM2M service layer, IETF CoAP and LoRaWAN specification if you want primary sources.
